title: Wet and dry waste: which bin, and where does it go?

summary.text: A dry onion skin goes in the wet waste bin. A milk packet with milk still inside goes in the dry waste bin. So the names wet and dry cannot mean how a thing feels. Wet waste is waste that rots, like peels and leftover food. Dry waste does not rot quickly, like plastic, paper, glass and metal. In this unit you press waste between paper napkins to see which leaves a wet mark, weigh one meal's waste on a hanger, and follow your bins to where they go.
summary.art: Two bins side by side, a green one with peels, onion skins and a dry leaf, and a blue one with a rinsed milk packet, a newspaper and a tin, with a child pointing at the dry leaf in the green bin.

intro.hook: Hold a dry onion skin in one hand and a banana peel in the other. Which one feels wet? Now guess. Which bin does each one go in?
intro.text: The banana peel feels wet. The onion skin feels dry and papery. Yet both go in the same bin, the wet waste bin. Wet waste means waste that rots. So how can you tell which bin a thing goes in, if feeling it does not tell you? Your napkin test will help you find out.
intro.art: A child's two hands, one holding a shiny wet banana peel and one holding a crackly brown onion skin, with a question mark between them.

outcomes: By the end I can say what wet waste and dry waste are, and give three examples of each.
By the end I can put everyday things in the right bin, even tricky ones like a dry leaf or a dirty milk packet.
By the end I can test which waste leaves a wet mark, and say why the mark does not decide the bin.
By the end I can compare one meal's wet waste and dry waste by how heavy they are and how much space they take.
By the end I can say where wet waste and dry waste go after they leave my home.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: Things we throw away because we do not need them any more.
terms.example: Banana peels, an empty biscuit packet and old newspaper are all waste.
terms.art: A small heap of a banana peel, an empty biscuit packet and a folded newspaper.

terms.meaning: To be slowly eaten by tiny living beings, until the thing breaks down into soil.
terms.example: A tomato left in a warm corner for many days goes soft, grows fuzzy mould and starts to rot.
terms.art: Three tomatoes in a row: fresh, soft and wrinkled, and soft with white fuzzy mould.

terms.meaning: Waste that rots. It comes from plants or animals. It may feel wet or dry.
terms.example: Vegetable peels, leftover rice, used tea leaves, eggshells, old flowers and dry leaves.
terms.art: A green bin holding vegetable peels, used tea leaves, an old marigold garland and a dry leaf.

terms.meaning: Waste that does not rot quickly. Much of it can be made into new things if it is kept clean and dry.
terms.example: A rinsed milk packet, a newspaper, a glass jar, a tin and a cardboard box.
terms.art: A blue bin holding a rinsed milk packet, a newspaper, a glass jar and a cardboard box.

terms.meaning: To put things into groups, so that things that are alike go together.
terms.example: We sort waste into a wet bin and a dry bin.
terms.art: A child dropping a peel into a green bin with one hand and a paper into a blue bin with the other.

terms.meaning: A living being that eats dead plants and animals and turns them into soil. Bacteria, fungi and earthworms are decomposers.
terms.example: Fungi grow on an old bread crust and slowly eat it. That fuzzy mould is a fungus.
terms.art: A close-up of an earthworm in dark soil next to a bit of peel, with tiny dots for bacteria.

terms.meaning: Very tiny living beings, each made of one cell. They are far too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: Bacteria in curd turn milk into curd. Other bacteria in soil help peels rot.
terms.art: A bowl of curd, and a round magnifying circle showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: Dark, crumbly soil made when wet waste rots. Plants grow well in it.
terms.example: Many buildings put their peels in a compost pot, and later use the compost for their plants.
terms.art: A hand holding a scoop of dark crumbly compost over a pot with a tulsi plant.

terms.meaning: To make old things into new things. Old paper is soaked and pressed into new paper.
terms.example: Old newspapers can be made into new paper, egg trays and paper bags.
terms.art: An arrow going from a pile of old newspapers to a stack of egg trays and new paper bags.

terms.meaning: A person whose work is to collect waste from homes and take it away, often in a cart or a small truck.
terms.example: In many buildings, a waste collector comes every morning with a cart that has a green drum and a blue drum.
terms.art: A woman waste collector in a sari and gloves pushing a handcart with a green drum and a blue drum.

terms.meaning: A big open place where a town's waste is thrown in a heap. Mixed waste often ends up there.
terms.example: A dump smells bad, and the heap can catch fire.
terms.art: A large grey heap of mixed waste with crows flying above it and smoke rising from one side.

explanations.context: This card explains what wet waste is, and why a dry leaf belongs with it.
explanations.definition: Wet waste is waste that rots. It comes from plants or animals: food, peels, shells, leaves and flowers.
explanations.description: Most kitchen scraps are wet, so wet waste got its name. But the real rule is that it rots. A peel, an onion skin and a dry leaf all came from plants, and decomposers slowly eat them. So a dry leaf goes in the wet bin, even though it feels dry.
examples: Peels of banana, potato, carrot and onion.
Leftover rice, idli, sambar or chapati.
Used tea leaves and filter coffee powder.
Eggshells, groundnut shells, old flowers and dry leaves.
explanations.art: A green bin with a peel, a groundnut shell, a dry leaf and some leftover rice, and tiny decomposers drawn near them.

explanations.concept: Dry waste: waste that does not rot quickly
explanations.context: This card explains what dry waste is, and why a wet milk packet still belongs with it.
explanations.definition: Dry waste is waste that does not rot quickly, like plastic, paper, glass, metal and cloth.
explanations.description: Decomposers cannot easily eat plastic, glass or metal, so these do not rot quickly. Much dry waste can be recycled, which means made into new things, but only if it is clean and dry. So a milk packet with milk inside must be rinsed and dried first. Paper comes from trees, but it goes in the dry bin, because clean paper can be made into new paper.
examples: A rinsed milk packet or oil packet.
A glass jar, a tin, a steel lid.
explanations.art: A blue bin with a rinsed milk packet drying on a tap, a newspaper, a glass jar and a tin.

explanations.context: This card explains what happens to the waste from our bins after it leaves home.
explanations.definition: Waste does not disappear when it leaves home. Sorted wet waste can go to a compost place. Sorted dry waste can go to a sorting shed and then for recycling. Mixed waste often goes to a dump.
explanations.description: A waste collector takes the bins from your home. In many cities, wet waste goes to a compost place, where decomposers turn it into compost for plants. Dry waste goes to a sorting shed, where workers, many of them women, sort it into paper, plastic, glass and metal to be sold and made into new things. Mixed waste is hard to use, so it often goes to a dump outside the town.
examples: Peels from a sorted green bin can become compost in a few weeks.
A rinsed milk packet from a blue bin can be sold and made into new plastic things.
A bag of mixed waste usually goes to the dump.
explanations.art: A picture map: a home in the middle, one road to a compost place with plants, one road to a sorting shed where women sort paper and bottles, and a dashed road from a mixed bag to a smoking dump.

explanations.context: This card is about dry leaves, a thing people do not all agree about.
explanations.description: Dry leaves rot, so most city guides say they go with wet waste. Some people burn them, and some cities collect leaves separately. People still argue about the best way.
examples: A dry leaf from a potted plant can go in the wet bin or in a compost pot.
Burning a heap of leaves makes thick smoke.

perspectives.explanation: Dry leaves rot like peels, so they go in the green bin, with wet waste.
Dry leaves are best kept in a separate bag. A handful mixed with wet peels each day stops the compost from getting slimy and smelly.
Burning leaves is quick. But the smoke is bad for everyone's lungs, so many cities ask people not to burn leaves.

explanations.art: A pile of dry leaves with three arrows: one to a green bin, one to a separate bag beside a compost pot, and one to a small fire crossed out.

agreed.text: Things from plants and animals, like peels, food and leaves, rot, because decomposers eat them.
agreed.evidence: A tomato or a bread crust left out for a week grows mould and goes soft. The mould is a fungus eating it.

agreed.text: Plastic, glass and metal stay the same for a very long time.
agreed.evidence: A plastic wrapper found in a drain can still be read years after it was thrown away. Glass bottles hundreds of years old are found whole.

agreed.text: Sorting at home makes waste much easier to use.
agreed.evidence: Clean, dry paper and plastic can be sold and recycled. Paper soaked with food cannot be made into good paper.

challenging.claim: Wet waste is anything that feels wet.
challenging.for: Most kitchen waste, like peels and leftover rice, is wet, so the name seems to fit.
challenging.against: A dry onion skin or a dry leaf goes in the wet bin, because it rots. A wet milk packet goes in the dry bin, because plastic does not rot. The napkin test shows this.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make about the names wet and dry.

challenging.claim: Once waste is in the dustbin, it is gone.
challenging.for: We do not see our waste again after the collector takes it, so it seems to have gone away.
challenging.against: Waste always goes somewhere: to a compost place, a sorting shed or a dump. A dump near a town can smell, catch fire and spoil the water under it.
challenging.context: This card is about what happens after the waste leaves home.

challenging.claim: Paper comes from trees, so paper is wet waste.
challenging.who: A clever guess some children make
challenging.for: Paper is made from wood, and wet paper does rot, slowly.
challenging.against: Clean paper is more useful made into new paper than rotted. So cities ask for paper in the dry bin. Paper soaked with food, like a greasy dosa wrapper, can go with wet waste.
challenging.context: This card is about paper, which comes from a plant but goes in the dry bin.

big_questions.q: Why does a dry onion skin go in the wet bin?
big_questions.hint: Think about what will happen to it next. Will it rot?

big_questions.q: Which tiny living beings eat our peels, and how do they find them?
big_questions.hint: Think about the fuzzy mould on old bread.

big_questions.q: Where does your waste go after the collector takes it away?
big_questions.hint: Ask the collector, or a grown-up who knows.

big_questions.q: Is anything really thrown away, or does it always go somewhere?
big_questions.hint: Follow one peel and one packet as far as you can.

big_questions.q: Is a peel waste for a worm?
big_questions.hint: What is it to us, and what is it to the worm?

story.title: Thangam Akka's Two Drums
story.note: Kavya, her Paati, Arun, Appa, Thangam Akka and Muniyamma are made up. Kodungaiyur is a real waste dump in Chennai. Many Indian cities use a green bin for wet waste and a blue bin for dry waste.
text: Kavya lived on the third floor of a building in Chennai. She was seven. Every morning at seven o'clock, the bell rang twice. That was Thangam Akka, who collected the waste.
Thangam Akka pushed a cart with two big drums on it. One drum was green. One drum was blue. She wore a bright orange sari and thick yellow gloves, and she knew every child in the building by name.
Kavya's family had two bins in the kitchen, a small green one and a small blue one. Kavya's Paati, her grandmother, had stuck a picture on each. A peel on the green bin. A newspaper on the blue bin.
One morning Kavya ran to the door with both bins. Thangam Akka tipped the green bin into the green drum. Then she lifted the blue bin, looked inside, and stopped.
'Kavya,' she said, 'what is this?' She held up a dry brown leaf from the tulsi pot on the balcony.
'That is dry,' said Kavya. 'So I put it in the dry bin.'
Thangam Akka smiled. 'Feel it. Yes, it is dry. But tell me. If you leave this leaf in a pot of soil, what will happen to it?'
Kavya thought. 'It will go soft. Then it will go into the soil.'

'It will rot,' said Thangam Akka. 'Tiny living beings in the soil will eat it. Anything that rots goes in the green drum. Dry leaves, onion skins, groundnut shells, even eggshells. They all came from plants or animals, and they all rot.'
She dropped the leaf into the green drum. Then she pulled out a milk packet from the blue bin. It was dripping.

'And this,' she said, 'is the opposite trouble. A milk packet is plastic. It does not rot, so it is dry waste. But you did not rinse it. Milk will drip onto the newspapers, and they will go sour and soggy. Nobody can make new paper from soggy paper.'
Kavya looked at the newspaper at the bottom of the bin. One corner was already wet and smelly.
'Where do the drums go?' Kavya asked.

'The green drum goes to the compost place behind the ward office,' said Thangam Akka. 'In a few weeks, the peels turn into dark soil. The park gardener puts it under the trees. The blue drum goes to the sorting shed. My friend Muniyamma and the other women there sort it into paper, plastic, glass and tins. Then it is sold, and made into new things.'
'And if I mix them?' asked Kavya.

'Then the shed cannot use it, and the compost place cannot use it. It goes to the big dump at Kodungaiyur. There it sits in a heap for years. It smells, and sometimes it burns.' Thangam Akka shook her head. 'Your waste does not vanish, Kavya. It only goes where you send it.'
That evening, Appa came home and threw a banana peel in the blue bin, and a dry pen with no ink in the green bin. Kavya's little brother Arun laughed.
Kavya did not laugh. She stood next to the bins like a teacher.
'Appa,' she said, 'there is a test. Ask: will it rot? A peel rots, so it goes in green. A pen does not rot, so it goes in blue. And if it is a packet, rinse it first.'
Appa moved the peel and the pen. Then he asked, 'And what about this dry onion skin?'
'Will it rot?' asked Kavya.
Appa thought for a moment. 'Yes,' he said, and put it in the green bin.
The next morning, the bell rang twice. Thangam Akka looked in both bins and gave Kavya a thumbs up with her yellow glove.
story.epiphany: A bin is chosen by asking what will happen to a thing next. If it will rot, it goes in the wet bin, even when it feels dry. Waste never vanishes. It goes where we send it.
ask: Why did the dry leaf belong in the green drum?
What went wrong with the milk packet?
Where does the green drum go, and where does the blue drum go?
What question did Kavya teach Appa to ask?
art: A woman waste collector in an orange sari and yellow gloves at a flat door, holding up a dry brown leaf, while a girl holds a green bin and a blue bin.
A girl standing beside two kitchen bins like a teacher, while her father holds a banana peel and a pen, and her little brother laughs.

games.title: Two Roads: a board game about where waste goes
games.context: This is a board game about sorting waste. Players pick a waste card, say which bin it goes in, and move along the road from home to a clean town.

printables.title: A board of 12 squares to draw or cut out
items: Square 4: Oops! A bag of mixed waste. Go back 1 square.
Square 6: The compost place. Peels turn into soil.
Square 8: The sorting shed. Women sort paper, plastic and tins.
Square 9: Oops! Someone burnt leaves. Miss a turn.
Square 10: New paper is made from old paper.
Square 11: Compost goes under a tree.
Square 12: A clean town. The first player here wins.

items.b: Wet bin. It rots.
Wet bin. It feels dry, but it rots.
Dry bin. Plastic does not rot.

items.f: Milk packet with milk inside (star card)
items.b: Rinse it first. Then dry bin.
Dry bin. It can be made into new paper.
Wet bin. It rots.
Wet bin. They rot.

items.f: Dry leaf from a pot (star card)
items.b: Wet bin. It feels dry, but it rots.
Dry bin. Glass does not rot.
Dry bin. Metal does not rot.
Wet bin. They feel dry, but they rot.
Wet bin. It rots slowly.
Wet bin. Flowers rot. Take out the thread first.
Dry bin. It can be made into new cardboard.
Dry bin. Paper, plastic and foil stuck together do not rot quickly.
Wet bin. It rots, slowly.
Dry bin. Cloth can be reused as rags.
Dry bin. Plastic does not rot.

items.f: Curry leaves left on the plate
items.b: Wet bin. They rot.

items.f: Dosa wrapped in greasy paper (star card)
items.b: Greasy paper is soaked with food, so it goes with wet waste.

rules: Draw or cut out the 12-square board. Put a small token for each player on Home.
Shuffle the waste cards. Put them face down in a pile.
On your turn, pick the top card and read the front aloud.
Say which bin it goes in: wet or dry. Say why.
Turn the card over. If you were right, move forward 1 square. If it was a star card and you were right, move forward 2 squares.
If you were wrong, stay where you are, and read the back aloud.
If you land on an Oops square, do what it says.
The first player to reach Square 12, the clean town, wins.

setup.art: A hand-drawn board of 12 squares in a winding road, from a house to a clean town with trees, with two tokens on the house.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the road of 12 squares. Put the tokens on Home.

setup.art: A child holding up a card that says 'Dry onion skin' and pointing to a green bin drawn on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Pick a card. Say wet or dry, and why. Move if you are right.

flow.do: 1. Draw the 12 squares on a sheet of paper, or cut them out. 2. Cut out the 20 cards. 3. Give each player a token, like a button.
flow.say: This road goes from our home to a clean town. You move when you sort a card the right way.
flow.kid: Put your token on Home. Shuffle the cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns picking a card. 2. Each player says wet or dry, and why. 3. Turn the card over and move.
flow.say: Groundnut shells. They feel dry. Will they rot? Which bin?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Ask: will it rot? Say wet or dry.

ask.q: Why did you put the groundnut shells in the wet bin?
good: Because they rot, even though they are dry.
Because they come from a plant.

flow.parent: The star cards are the tricky ones. Let your child think aloud. Praise the reason, not only the answer.

check.q: Which bin does a dry leaf go in?
options: The wet bin, because it rots
The dry bin, because it feels dry
check.why: A dry leaf came from a plant, and decomposers eat it. Things that rot go in the wet bin, even if they feel dry.

flow.do: Ask which card was the hardest, and why.
flow.say: Which card was hardest to sort? What helped you choose?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? What helped you?

experiments.title: The Napkin Press Test: is wet waste always wet?
experiments.context: In this experiment you press eight kinds of waste between paper napkins under a heavy book. Then you look for wet marks, and compare them with the bin each thing goes in.
experiments.question: Which kinds of waste leave a wet mark on a paper napkin? Do all the things that go in the wet bin leave a wet mark?
experiments.predict: Look at the eight things and touch each one. Which ones will leave a wet mark on the napkin? Why do you think so? Then say which bin each one goes in.
experiments.fair_test: Every piece is about the size of a one-rupee coin. Every piece sits on the same kind of napkin, under the same heavy book, for the same time, 10 minutes. Only the kind of waste is different.
results_table: Which bin does it go in?

materials.item: a small piece of banana peel or potato peel, inside facing down
a spoon of leftover cooked rice, spread flat
a spoon of used tea leaves or filter coffee powder
a dry onion skin
a dry leaf from a potted plant, or two or three groundnut shells
a piece of an empty milk packet with a few drops of milk still in it, not rinsed
a piece of a dry plastic wrapper, like a biscuit packet
a piece of dry newspaper
8 paper napkins or squares of pale tissue
a big tray or an old newspaper to work on
a heavy book, or a steel plate with a full water bottle on it
a pencil, to write a number on each napkin
a folded tea towel or old cloth, to lay over the napkins

experiments.safety: Wash hands with soap after touching the waste. Use a peel from today's cooking, not old smelly waste. Leave out glass and sharp tin edges.

schedule.what: Touch and guess. Press the eight pieces under a book for 10 minutes. Look for wet marks. Sort them into bins.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the two napkins that surprised you most. Circle the things that went in the wet bin but left no wet mark.

setup.art: Eight napkins laid in two rows on a tray, each with a number, and a small piece of waste on each: peel, rice, tea leaves, onion skin, dry leaf, milk packet, wrapper, newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Put one piece on each numbered napkin.

setup.art: Each piece covered with a second napkin, and a heavy book pressing down on top of all of them.
setup.caption: 2. Fold each napkin over its piece. Cover with a cloth and press with a heavy book for 10 minutes.

setup.art: The book lifted and the pieces removed, showing wet grey spots on some napkins and clean white napkins under the onion skin, dry leaf, wrapper and newspaper.
setup.caption: 3. Lift the book. Which napkins have a wet mark?

setup.art: The napkins sorted into a green box and a blue box drawn on paper, with the onion skin and dry leaf napkins clean but in the green box.
setup.caption: 4. Sort the napkins by bin. Which ones surprise you?

flow.do: 1. Lay out the eight pieces of waste. 2. Let your child touch each one. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Touch each one. Which ones will leave a wet mark on a napkin? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Touch each thing. Which will leave a wet mark? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the onion skin will or will not leave a mark?
good: No mark, because it feels dry and papery.
Maybe a mark, because it comes from an onion, and onions are juicy.

flow.parent: Write the guesses down word for word. Don't say if they are right. The test will answer.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Napkin Press Test. You touch eight kinds of waste and guess which will leave a wet mark.

flow.do: 1. Write the numbers 1 to 8 on eight napkins. 2. Lay them on the tray. 3. Put one piece on each napkin and fold the napkin over it. 4. Lay a folded cloth over all eight. 5. Put the heavy book on top.
flow.say: Every piece is the same size. Every piece gets the same book on top. Then only the kind of waste is different.
flow.kid: Put one piece on each napkin. Cover them. Put the book on top.
flow.parent: Put the peel inside face down. The cloth makes thick and thin pieces press the same. If the book is too small, use a steel plate with a full bottle on it.

flow.do: 1. Wait 10 minutes. 2. While you wait, ask the question below. 3. Then lift the book and take the pieces off. 4. Hold each napkin up to the light.
flow.say: While we wait, tell me. Which bin does each one go in? Now let's lift the book. Which napkins have a wet mark?
flow.kid: Wait ten minutes. Say which bin each one goes in. Then lift the book. Look for wet marks.

good: The peel, the rice, the tea leaves and the milk packet.
The onion skin and the dry leaf left no mark.

flow.parent: The peel, rice and tea leaves usually leave a clear damp grey patch. The unrinsed milk packet leaves white drops. The onion skin, dry leaf, wrapper and newspaper leave the napkin clean and dry.

check.q: Why does every piece get the same book and the same time?
options: So the test is fair, and only the kind of waste is different
Because we have only one book
So the napkins do not blow away
check.why: If one piece were pressed longer or harder, it might leave a bigger mark only because of that. With the same book and time, any difference comes from the waste.

flow.do: 1. Put the napkins in two groups: wet bin and dry bin. 2. Ask your child what they see. 3. Ask them to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Look at the wet bin group. Did every one leave a wet mark? So what decides the bin? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the wet bin group. Are all of them wet? What decides the bin?

ask.q: Why does the dry onion skin go in the wet bin?
good: Because it rots, even if it is dry.
Because it comes from a plant, and tiny living beings eat it.

ask.q: Why does the wet milk packet go in the dry bin?
good: Because it is plastic, and plastic does not rot.
But we must rinse it first.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses what they saw: 'The onion skin left no mark, but it still goes in the wet bin, because it rots.' Read the card 'Wet waste: waste that rots' only after your child has had their say.

experiments.title: The Hanger Balance: is our wet waste or dry waste heavier?
experiments.context: In this experiment you keep the waste from one meal in two bags, one wet and one dry. You hang them from the two ends of a clothes hanger, and see which side goes down. Then you see which bag takes more space.
experiments.question: After one meal, which is heavier: our wet waste or our dry waste? And which one takes up more space?
experiments.predict: Look at the two bags before you hang them. Which one will be heavier? Which one looks bigger? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both bags are the same kind of bag, and the waste comes from the same meal. Both bags hang from the same hanger, at the very ends, the same distance from the hook.
results_table: Number of things in the bag

materials.item: the wet waste from cooking and eating one meal, like peels, leftover food and tea leaves
the dry waste from the same meal and day, like packets, wrappers, a paper bag or a box
two plastic bags or cloth bags of the same kind and size
a plastic or wire clothes hanger with a notch or bar at each end
two pieces of string, each about 20 cm long
a door handle or a curtain rod to hang the hanger from
a steel tumbler

experiments.safety: Wash hands with soap after handling the waste. Tie the wet bag shut so nothing drips. Leave glass, tins and other sharp things out of the bags.

schedule.what: Keep one meal's waste in two bags. Guess. Hang them on the hanger. Count the things. Fill tumblers to compare space.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the hanger, and show which side went down.

setup.art: A clothes hanger hanging from a door handle, with a string loop at each end of its bar.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a hanger from a door handle.

setup.art: A bag of peels and leftover food on one end of the hanger and a bag of packets and a small box on the other end, with the wet side hanging lower.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the wet bag on one end and the dry bag on the other.

setup.art: A child pressing packets into a steel tumbler and counting tumblers, with a row of tally marks beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Count the things. Fill tumblers to see which takes more space.

flow.do: 1. After one meal, keep the wet waste in one bag and the dry waste in the other. 2. Show both bags to your child. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Here is the waste from our lunch. Which bag will be heavier? Which one looks bigger? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the two bags. Which is heavier? Which is bigger? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that bag is heavier?
good: The wet one, because wet things are heavy.
The dry one, because it is bigger.

flow.parent: Write the guesses down. Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Tie a string loop at each end of the hanger. 2. Hang the hanger from a door handle. 3. Check that it hangs level when empty. 4. Hang the wet bag from one loop and the dry bag from the other.
flow.say: When nothing hangs on it, the hanger is level. Now watch. Which side goes down?
flow.kid: Hang one bag on each end. Watch. Which side goes down?
flow.parent: If the empty hanger tips, slide one string loop until it hangs level. The heavier bag goes down. In most Indian homes the wet bag goes down, because peels and food hold a lot of water.

flow.do: 1. Take the bags down. 2. Empty each bag on a tray, one at a time. 3. Count the things in each and make tally marks. 4. Put the waste back in its bag.
flow.say: Let's count. Make a tally mark for each thing. Which bag has more things?
flow.kid: Count the things in each bag. Make a tally mark for each one.
flow.parent: Count a heap of rice or tea leaves as one thing. Wash hands after this step.

flow.do: 1. Press the dry waste into the tumbler, one tumbler at a time, and count. 2. Do the same with the wet waste, using a spoon. 3. Write both numbers.
flow.say: Now let's see which takes more space. How many tumblers does each bag fill?
flow.kid: Fill the tumbler again and again. Count how many for each bag.

good: The dry bag, because packets are light but big.
The wet bag.

flow.parent: Dry waste is often light but takes a lot of space, because packets and boxes are full of air. Wet waste is often heavy but small. Your home may be different, and that is a result too.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: So which is heavier, and which takes more space? What did you see? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Which was heavier? Which was bigger? Why?

ask.q: Why can a small bag be heavier than a big bag?
good: Because the wet things have a lot of water in them.
Because the packets are light and full of air.

check.q: On the hanger, which bag goes down?
check.why: A hanger balance tips towards the heavier side. A big bag of light packets can rise while a small bag of wet peels goes down.

activities.title: Kitchen Sort: two steel bowls
activities.context: In this activity you sort the scraps from cooking into two steel bowls, wet and dry, while a grown-up cooks.

materials.item: two steel bowls or plates
two slips of paper: one with a green peel drawn on it, one with a blue newspaper drawn on it
the waste from cooking one meal

schedule.what: Sort the cooking waste into a wet bowl and a dry bowl. Then empty the bowls into the home bins.

activities.record: Draw the two bowls and what went in each.

setup.art: Two steel bowls on a kitchen counter, one marked with a green peel and one with a blue newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Put out two bowls and label them.

setup.art: A child dropping a carrot peel into the green bowl and an empty dal packet into the blue bowl, while a woman cooks at the stove.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each scrap as it comes. Ask: will it rot?

flow.do: 1. Put the two bowls near the counter, away from the stove. 2. Put a label by each bowl.
flow.say: Green is for things that rot. Blue is for things that do not rot quickly.
flow.kid: Green is for things that rot. Blue is for the rest.

flow.do: 1. As you cook, hand each scrap to your child. 2. Let them choose a bowl. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Here is the onion skin. Will it rot? Which bowl?
flow.kid: Take each scrap. Ask: will it rot? Put it in a bowl.

ask.q: Where does the dal packet go?
good: Blue, because it is plastic and does not rot.
Blue, after we shake out the dal dust.

flow.parent: Keep your child away from the stove and knives. Hand them the scraps.

flow.do: Empty each bowl into the matching home bin, and wash the bowls.
flow.say: Now the green bowl goes in the green bin, and the blue bowl in the blue bin.
flow.kid: Empty each bowl into its bin. Wash your hands.

activities.title: Watch the Waste Leave: who takes it, and where to?
activities.context: In this activity you watch your waste being collected, and find out where the wet and dry waste go. Then you draw a map of the two roads.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and crayons
your home's waste bins on collection day

schedule.what: Watch the waste collector come. Ask one question. Draw the map of where wet and dry waste go.

activities.record: A map with your home in the middle, a green road for wet waste and a blue road for dry waste.

setup.art: A child and her mother at a flat door, handing two bins to a woman waste collector with a cart that has two drums.
setup.caption: 1. Hand over the bins. Look at the cart.

setup.art: A child's crayon map: a house in the middle, a green road to a compost place with plants, and a blue road to a shed with bottles and papers.
setup.caption: 2. Draw where each road goes.

flow.do: 1. When the collector comes, go to the door with your child. 2. Look at the cart or truck together. 3. Count how many parts it has.
flow.say: Look at the cart. Does it keep wet and dry waste apart? How many drums or parts can you count?
flow.kid: Look at the cart. How many parts does it have? Are wet and dry apart?
flow.parent: Many carts have two drums or a truck with two sections. If yours has only one, that is worth noticing too. Greet the collector by name, and thank them.

flow.do: Help your child ask the collector one short question, if the collector has time.
flow.say: Let's ask where the green drum goes, and where the blue drum goes.
flow.kid: Ask: where does the wet waste go? Where does the dry waste go?
flow.parent: If the collector is busy, ask your building secretary or look on your city's website later. Some cities send wet waste to a compost place and dry waste to a sorting shed.

flow.do: 1. Give your child paper and crayons. 2. Ask them to draw their home in the middle. 3. Then a green road and a blue road, and where each ends.
flow.say: Draw our home in the middle. Where does the green road go? Where does the blue road go? What happens to mixed waste?
flow.kid: Draw your home. Draw a green road and a blue road. Where do they end?

ask.q: What happens at the end of the green road?
good: The peels rot and turn into compost.
The compost helps plants grow.

activities.title: Rinse It, Dry It: getting a milk packet ready
activities.context: In this activity you get an empty milk packet ready for the dry bin, by rinsing and drying it.

materials.item: an empty milk packet, curd packet or oil packet
a little water in a mug
a clothes peg or a tap to hang it on

schedule.what: Rinse the packet. Hang it to dry. Put it in the dry bin the next day.

activities.record: Draw the packet before and after rinsing.

setup.art: A child pouring a little water into a cut milk packet over a sink and swishing it.
setup.caption: 1. Pour in a little water. Swish. Pour it out.

setup.art: A rinsed milk packet hanging from a clothes peg on a balcony line.
setup.caption: 2. Hang it up to dry.

flow.do: 1. Cut the packet fully open along one side with scissors. 2. Let your child pour in a little water and swish it. 3. Pour the water into a plant pot or the sink.
flow.say: Why do we rinse it? What would the milk do to the newspapers in the dry bin?
flow.kid: Pour in a little water. Swish it. Pour it out.

good: So the milk does not make the paper wet and smelly.
So it can be sold and recycled.

flow.parent: The milky rinse water can go into a plant pot. A grown-up does the cutting.

flow.do: 1. Hang the packet on a peg or tap to dry. 2. The next day, put it flat in the dry bin.
flow.say: When it is dry, it is ready. Clean and dry is what the sorting shed needs.
flow.kid: Hang it up. When it is dry, put it in the dry bin.

challenges.title: A Bin Label Everyone Can Read
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make labels for your home's two bins that everyone can use, even someone who cannot read English.
challenges.problem: Make one label for the wet bin and one for the dry bin. Everyone at home must know which bin to use, from Paati to a visitor who reads another language.
constraints: Use only paper, crayons or pictures cut from old magazines.
At most 5 words on each label.
Each label must show at least one tricky thing, like a dry leaf or a rinsed packet.
materials: two sheets of paper or card
general: A green label with a drawn peel, and a blue label with a drawn newspaper.
The words WET and DRY in big letters.
creative: A label with the question 'Will it rot?' and a tick or a cross.
Labels in English and in the language your family speaks at home, like Tamil, Telugu, Bengali or Marathi.
A drawing of a worm on the green label, to show who eats the waste.
challenges.your_turn: Make your labels and stick them on. Ask someone at home to sort five things using only your labels. If they make a mistake, change the label.

setup.art: A child drawing a peel, an onion skin and a dry leaf on a green card, with crayons around.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your label for the wet bin.

setup.art: A grandmother sorting a dry leaf into a green bin with a child's picture label stuck on it.
setup.caption: 2. Stick it on. Watch someone use it.

flow.do: Read the challenge. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Who at home might find the bins confusing? What would help them?
flow.kid: Who might put things in the wrong bin? What would help them?

flow.do: Let your child make the two labels. Help only with cutting and sticking.
flow.say: Remember the napkin test. Which tricky things should your label show?
flow.kid: Make your labels. Show one tricky thing on each.

flow.do: 1. Stick the labels on the bins. 2. Give someone at home five things to sort. 3. Watch.
flow.say: Let's see if your labels work. Did anyone make a mistake? What will you change?
flow.kid: Watch someone sort five things. Did your labels help? What will you change?

items.p: Sort these into the wet bin and the dry bin.
items.why: Peels, tea leaves and eggshells rot, so they are wet waste. Glass, paper and metal do not rot quickly, so they are dry waste.

items.p: In the Napkin Press Test, which piece left no wet mark but still goes in the wet bin?
items.why: The onion skin is dry, so it left the napkin clean. But it rots, so it goes in the wet bin. Picking the plastic wrapper may mean thinking 'no mark' means 'wet bin'.
items.context: This question is about the Napkin Press Test. You press peels, shells, packets and paper between paper napkins under a heavy book, and look for wet marks.

items.p: Draw two napkins from the Napkin Press Test: one with a wet mark, and one with no mark. Write what was on each.
items.a: One napkin with a grey patch, labelled peel, rice or tea leaves. One clean napkin, labelled onion skin, dry leaf, wrapper or newspaper.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the mark clearly and names the waste. The best ones pick a clean napkin from the wet bin group, like the onion skin.
items.context: This question is about the Napkin Press Test. You press peels, shells, packets and paper between paper napkins under a heavy book, and look for wet marks.
items.art: Two empty squares side by side for drawing napkins.

items.p: Everything in the wet bin feels wet.
items.why: False. Dry leaves, onion skins and groundnut shells feel dry, but they rot, so they go in the wet bin.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: waste that does not rot quickly
to be eaten by tiny living beings until it turns into soil
dark soil made from rotted wet waste
items.why: These are the four words the child needs to sort waste and say where it goes.

items.p: Three of these go in the wet bin. Which one goes in the dry bin?
items.why: A plastic pen does not rot. The other three came from plants and rot.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: what question can you ask to choose the bin for any waste?
items.a: Will it rot? If yes, the wet bin. If no, the dry bin.
items.why: A strong answer asks about what happens to the thing next, not how it feels.

items.p: Label each picture: wet bin or dry bin.
items.why: The leaf and the flowers rot. The packet is plastic, and the box can be made into new cardboard.
items.art: Four small pictures with an empty label under each.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 2 in Madurai, threw away 4 peels, 2 packets, 1 tin and 3 eggshells. How many things went in the wet bin?
items.why: The peels and eggshells rot. 4 peels and 3 eggshells make 7. The packets and the tin go in the dry bin.

items.p: Where does sorted wet waste go in many cities?
opts: To a compost place, where it turns into soil
To a shop to be sold
items.why: Wet waste rots, so it can be made into compost for plants. Picking 'a shop' mixes it up with dry waste, which can be sold.

items.p: Tiny living beings that eat dead plants and turn them into soil are called ____.
items.why: Bacteria, fungi and earthworms are decomposers.

items.p: Your milk packet still has milk in it. Say what you will do before it goes in the dry bin, and why.
items.a: Rinse it and let it dry, so the milk does not make the paper in the dry bin wet and smelly.
items.why: A strong answer gives both the action and the reason: clean, dry waste can be recycled.

items.p: Two girls in Class 2 argue about a dry leaf from the balcony.

views.says: It is dry, so it goes in the dry bin.
It will rot, so it goes in the wet bin.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the Napkin Press Test to say why. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Sana: the dry leaf left no wet mark, but it rots, so it goes in the wet bin. It also says Lakshmi is right that the leaf is dry to touch.
items.why: Both girls notice something true. The test shows the leaf is dry, and the bin depends on whether it rots.

items.p: On the Hanger Balance, the small wet bag went down and the big dry bag went up. Why?
opts: The wet bag was heavier, because peels and food hold water
items.why: A hanger tips towards the heavier side. Packets are big but light. Picking 'the big bag' may mean thinking bigger is always heavier.
items.context: This question is about the Hanger Balance. You hang one meal's wet waste and dry waste from the two ends of a clothes hanger, and see which side goes down.

items.p: Put the journey of a banana peel in order.
items: The peel goes in the green bin at home.
The waste collector takes the green bin.
The peel goes to a compost place.
It becomes compost under a tree.
items.why: The peel leaves home sorted, reaches a compost place, and is eaten until it becomes soil.

items.p: Draw what happens to a bag of mixed waste, with peels and packets together. Where does it end up?
items.a: A bag going to a big heap at a dump, perhaps with crows, flies or smoke.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that mixed waste cannot easily go to the compost place or the sorting shed, so it often goes to a dump.

items.p: When the waste collector takes our bin, the waste is gone for ever.
items.why: False. Waste always goes somewhere: a compost place, a sorting shed or a dump.

items.p: Paper comes from trees, but it goes in the dry bin. Say why.
items.a: Because clean paper can be made into new paper. If it got wet and rotted, it could not be used again.
items.why: A strong answer says that the dry bin is for things that can be made into new things, and paper is one of them.

items.p: Label the map: write compost place, sorting shed or dump at the end of each road.
items.why: Sorted wet waste goes to compost, sorted dry waste to a sorting shed, and mixed waste often to a dump.
items.art: A home in the middle with a green road, a blue road and a grey dashed road, each ending in an empty box.

items.p: Teja, a girl in Class 2, filled 5 tumblers with her dry waste and 2 tumblers with her wet waste. How many more tumblers did the dry waste fill?
items.why: 5 take away 2 is 3. The dry waste took more space, even though the wet waste may be heavier.
items.context: This question is about the Hanger Balance. You hang one meal's wet waste and dry waste from the two ends of a clothes hanger, and see which side goes down.

items.p: Mou, a girl in Class 2 in Kolkata, has finished a dosa that came wrapped in greasy paper. Which bin is best for the greasy paper?
opts: The wet bin, because it is soaked with food and will rot
The dry bin, because all paper is dry waste
items.why: Paper soaked with food cannot be made into new paper, but it rots with the food. Burning makes smoke that is bad for everyone's lungs.

items.p: Many people think waste is wet waste if it feels wet. What test would you do to show a friend this is not always true?
items.a: Press a dry onion skin and a peel between napkins under a book. The onion skin leaves no mark, but it still rots, so it goes in the wet bin.
items.why: A strong answer names a real test and says what result would show the idea is wrong.

items.p: Match each worker to the job.
pairs: sorts dry waste into paper, plastic, glass and tins
eat wet waste and turn it into soil
items.why: People and other living beings all work on our waste. Decomposers are living beings too.

quiz.why: Wet waste is waste that rots, like peels and food. Picking 'waste that is wet' is the common mix-up: a dry leaf is wet waste too.

quiz.p: Which of these is dry waste?
quiz.why: Glass does not rot. Rice and eggshells rot, so they are wet waste.

quiz.p: Which bin does a dry onion skin go in?
quiz.why: The onion skin feels dry, but it rots. So it goes in the wet bin.

quiz.p: Priya, a girl in Class 2, has a milk packet with milk still inside. What should she do?
opts: Rinse it, dry it, and put it in the dry bin
Put it in the wet bin, because it is wet
Put it in the dry bin with the milk inside
quiz.why: The packet is plastic, so it is dry waste. Rinsing stops the milk from spoiling the paper in the dry bin.

quiz.p: In the Napkin Press Test, which piece usually leaves a wet mark?
quiz.why: A peel is full of water, so it wets the napkin. Paper and dry leaves leave it clean.

quiz.p: The onion skin left no wet mark. What does this tell us?
opts: A wet mark does not decide the bin. Whether it rots does.
The onion skin goes in the dry bin
quiz.why: The onion skin is dry, but it rots. So the napkin mark does not tell us the bin.

quiz.p: On the Hanger Balance, which side goes down?
quiz.why: A hanger balance tips towards the heavier side. A big bag can be light.

quiz.p: Packets and boxes take a lot of space but are light. Why?
quiz.why: Packets and boxes hold air, so they are big but light. Peels hold water, so they are small but heavy.

quiz.p: Where does sorted dry waste go in many cities?
opts: To a sorting shed, then to be made into new things
quiz.why: Workers sort dry waste into paper, plastic, glass and metal, and sell it to be recycled.

quiz.p: Where does mixed waste often end up?
quiz.why: Mixed waste is hard to compost or recycle, so it often goes to a dump.

quiz.p: Nandini, a girl in Class 2, guesses the tea leaves will leave a wet mark. What should she do next?
opts: Test it, and see if she was right
Change her guess to be safe
quiz.why: A guess with a reason is a good start. The test tells us what really happens.

applications: Homes and buildings in many Indian cities keep a green bin for wet waste and a blue bin for dry waste.
Compost made from sorted wet waste is used in parks, farms and balcony pots.
Clean dry waste is sold to kabadiwalas and sorting centres, and made into new paper, plastic and metal things.
Some temples and wedding halls send old flowers to be made into compost.
Schools and railway stations put two coloured bins side by side.

spotted.text: A green bin and a blue bin side by side at a railway station or a bus stand.
spotted.art: A green bin and a blue bin on a railway platform, with a train in the background.

spotted.text: The waste collector's cart or truck with two drums or two parts, in Chennai, Pune, Indore and many other cities.
spotted.art: A small white truck with two sections, one marked wet and one marked dry, in a city lane.

spotted.text: A heap of old marigold and jasmine flowers after a festival like Onam, Ganesh Chaturthi or Durga Puja, waiting to rot.
spotted.art: A heap of old orange marigold and white jasmine flowers beside a temple wall.

spotted.text: A kabadiwala's shop stacked with bundles of newspaper, cardboard and bottles.
spotted.art: A small shop with tied bundles of newspaper, flattened cardboard boxes and sacks of bottles.

spotted.text: Fuzzy mould on an old bread crust or a forgotten lemon: decomposers at work.
spotted.art: A lemon with green and white fuzzy mould on one side.

open_questions.q: Can we find living beings that eat plastic quickly?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016, scientists in Japan described bacteria that can eat one kind of plastic, the kind used for water bottles. But they eat it very slowly. Nobody knows yet if any living being can eat most plastics quickly.

open_questions.q: How long does a dry leaf take to rot?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the leaf, the heat, the water and which decomposers are there. A soft leaf may rot in weeks, a tough one in months. Scientists still measure this for different leaves and places.

ask_kids: Will it rot? Ask that about the next thing you throw away.
What did we throw away today that was wet waste but felt dry?
Who takes our waste, and what is her name or his name?
Which do you think we throw away more of: wet waste or dry waste?
If our bin could talk, what would it say about where it goes?

jokes.j: Why did the onion skin go to the wet bin?
jokes.a: Because it knew it was going to rot, sooner or later.

jokes.j: What did the banana peel say to the napkin?
jokes.a: Sorry for leaving a mark on you!

jokes.j: Why was the milk packet so clean?
jokes.a: It had a good rinse before bed.

jokes.j: What did the dry leaf say to Kavya?
jokes.a: Don't judge me by how I feel!

jokes.j: Why did the worm love the green bin?
jokes.a: It was a full lunch box.

jokes.j: What did the hanger say to the bag of peels?
Why did the newspaper stay out of the wet bin?
jokes.a: It didn't want to get soggy news.

jokes.j: What did the tin say at the sorting shed?

maths.problem: In the Napkin Press Test, 8 pieces were pressed. 4 left a wet mark. How many left no mark?
maths.explain: 8 take away 4 is 4. So half the pieces left a mark and half did not.
maths.context: This question is about the Napkin Press Test. You press peels, shells, packets and paper between paper napkins under a heavy book, and look for wet marks.
maths.why_maths: Counting each group helps us see that the wet-mark group and the wet-bin group are not the same.

maths.problem: 5 things go in the wet bin: a peel, rice, tea leaves, an onion skin and a dry leaf. 3 of them left a wet mark. How many wet bin things left no mark?
maths.answer: 2: the onion skin and the dry leaf.
maths.explain: 5 take away 3 is 2. These two are the surprise: they rot, but they are dry.
maths.context: This question is about the Napkin Press Test. You press peels, shells, packets and paper between paper napkins under a heavy book, and look for wet marks.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference between the two groups shows exactly which things break the 'wet means wet' idea.

maths.problem: Farida, a girl in Class 2 in Pune, made tally marks: wet waste |||| ||, dry waste ||||. Which has more, and by how many?
maths.explain: |||| || is 7 and |||| is 4. 7 take away 4 is 3. So her family threw 3 more wet things than dry things.
maths.context: This question is about the Hanger Balance. You hang one meal's wet waste and dry waste from the two ends of a clothes hanger, and see which side goes down.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let us count waste as it comes, then compare the two bins at a glance.

maths.problem: On the Hanger Balance, the wet bag went down. But the dry bag filled 6 tumblers and the wet bag filled 2. Which bag takes more space? Does bigger always mean heavier?
maths.answer: The dry bag takes more space. No, bigger does not always mean heavier.
maths.explain: 6 is more than 2, so the dry bag is bigger. But the wet bag went down, so it is heavier. Packets are big and full of air. Peels are small and full of water.
maths.context: This question is about the Hanger Balance. You hang one meal's wet waste and dry waste from the two ends of a clothes hanger, and see which side goes down.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two ways, by weight and by space, shows that one number does not tell the whole story.

warmup.a: Waste that rots, like peels and food.

warmup.a: The wet bin, because it rots.

warmup.q: What should you do to a milk packet before the dry bin?

founder: ideas/by_topic/waste.md: the 'Waste is not a waste' week and the idea of seeing things differently, used for the roots and the question 'Will it rot?'. The Semmelweis SCI card fits handwashing and germs better than Class 2 sorting, so it was not used here.

NCERT Class 3 Our Wondrous World, chapter on waste: green bin for things that rot easily, including dried leaves and eggshells, and blue bin for metal, glass, plastic and paper. This unit leads into the Class 3 unit, which tests what wet waste does to dry waste.
science: Supreme Court of India, Almitra H. Patel and another versus Union of India, Writ Petition (Civil) 888 of 1996; the Barman Committee report of 1998; Municipal Solid Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000; Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, which ask every home to separate biodegradable, non-biodegradable and domestic hazardous waste.
S. Yoshida and others, 'A bacterium that degrades and assimilates poly(ethylene terephthalate)', Science 351 (2016), 1196-1199: Ideonella sakaiensis.
Decomposition of plant litter by bacteria and fungi: any ecology textbook.
Tao Te Ching 16. Thich Nhat Hanh's teaching on interbeing, the flower and the garbage.
sources.walkthrough: The Napkin Press Test was thought through for a city flat. A coin-sized piece of fresh banana or potato peel pressed inside face down, a spoon of cooked rice and a spoon of used tea leaves each leave a clear damp grey patch on a paper napkin within 10 minutes under a heavy book. An unrinsed milk packet leaves white drops. A dry onion skin, a dry leaf, a dry wrapper and newspaper leave the napkin dry. On the Hanger Balance, one meal's peels and leftovers usually outweigh its packets, but homes differ, and the step says so. The spine is the intro, the Napkin Press Test and the explanations (session 1, about 35 minutes), then the Kitchen Sort, Roots and the quiz (session 2, about 30 minutes).

roots.context: We have tested which waste leaves a wet mark and found that the mark does not decide the bin. Now we ask what that tells us about waste, about the beings who eat it, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In our test, the dry onion skin left no wet mark, but the milky packet did. Still, the onion skin goes in the wet bin and the packet in the dry bin. A bin is chosen by what can happen to a thing next. Wet waste rots into soil, and clean dry waste can often be made into new things.
deep_truth.habit: We name things by how they look or feel now, like wet and dry. The napkin test showed that how a thing feels today does not tell us what will become of it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Napkin Press Test, the peel, rice and tea leaves wet the napkin, and so did the unrinsed milk packet. The onion skin and the dry leaf left it dry. Yet the onion skin and the leaf rot, so they go in the wet bin. The packet does not rot, so after a rinse it goes in the dry bin.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who eats food and leaves peels. What you throw away becomes food for other living beings.
three.what_is_life: Bacteria, fungi and worms eat what is left of plants and animals. Their eating turns it back into soil, where new plants grow.
three.what_is_this_world: Nothing is ever thrown right out of the world. Every peel and every packet goes somewhere.

roots.thread: A peel was part of a living banana plant. In the bin, bacteria and fungi find the peel, choose it as food and eat it. Their bodies grow, and what is left becomes soil. New plants can grow in that soil. Plastic sits outside this circle for now, because almost no decomposer eats it.

teachings.teaching: All things grow and flourish, and then each one goes back to its root.
teachings.link: A peel goes back to the soil it came from, when decomposers eat it. That is what the green bin is for.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, teachings on interbeing
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a flower and you can see the compost it will become. Look deeply at compost and you can see the flowers it will grow.
teachings.link: The onion skin in the wet bin looks like rubbish. Looked at deeply, it is soil, and then a new plant.

science.text: Bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals, and return what was in them to the soil. Without them, dead leaves would pile up for ever.
In 2016, scientists in Japan described bacteria that can slowly eat one kind of plastic. Whether such living beings could ever deal with most of our plastic is still an open question.
Bacteria and fungi sense food and grow towards it. They are conscious beings, and thinking is not only done by brains.

other_view.view: They describe bacteria and fungi breaking down a peel as chemistry: the microbes make juices called enzymes that cut the peel into small pieces. They do not use the words choose or want for this.

practice.title: Where will it go?
practice.say: Hold one peel or one dry leaf in your open hand. Look at it slowly. Feel how heavy it is. Now close your eyes. Think of it going into the green bin. Think of it on the cart. Think of tiny living beings eating it. Think of it becoming dark soil, and a small plant growing there. Open your eyes. Put it in the green bin gently.
practice.kid: Hold a peel or a dry leaf. Look at it. Close your eyes. Think where it will go. Picture the soil. Picture a small plant. Open your eyes. Put it in the green bin.

ask: Is a peel waste for a worm?
If a thing will become soil, is it rubbish, or something else?
What do you throw away that might become part of a plant one day?
roots.art: A child holding a dry onion skin over a green bin, with a dotted path from the bin into the soil and up into a small green plant.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many towns in India took mixed garbage out of town and tipped it onto open land. Many people thought the problem was gone once it was out of sight. Almitra Patel, a scientist and campaigner near Bengaluru, looked at what those dumps were really like. They smelled and caught fire. Rain washed dirty water out of them, into the ground and into wells. She said cities must collect waste every day, keep wet and dry waste apart, and make compost from wet waste. In 1996 she took the problem to the Supreme Court of India. The court set up a committee to study it. Its work led to India's first national rules for city waste, in 2000. Rules from 2016 say every home must sort its waste. The dump was never the end of the waste. It only moved it somewhere else.
how_we_found_out.who: Almitra Patel, scientist and campaigner, near Bengaluru; the Supreme Court of India and its committee
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That taking mixed garbage out of town and dumping it solved the problem. Almitra Patel showed that dumps poison air, soil and water, and that sorting at home, collecting every day and composting wet waste work better.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in her sixties with short grey hair and a notebook, standing at the edge of a smoking garbage dump outside a town, writing down what she sees.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat today, with the materials listed. The Napkin Press Test uses only kitchen scraps, napkins and a heavy book, and the damp patches from peel, rice and tea leaves are easy to see within 10 minutes. The pieces are coin-sized so a single book presses all eight. The Hanger Balance works with an ordinary hanger on a door handle. The step tells the parent to level the empty hanger first, and says that homes may get different results. Watching the collector needs a grown-up at the door, and offers another way if the collector is busy. Cutting the milk packet is done by a grown-up. No item needs to be bought.
